title: Polynomial-Size Encoding of All Cuts of Small Value in Integer-Valued Symmetric Submodular Functions
classifications: Mathematics of computing → Matroids and greedoids
Theory of computation → Graph algorithms analysis
abstract: We study connectivity functions, that is, integer-valued symmetric submodular functions on a finite ground set attaining 0 on the empty set. For a connectivity function f on an n-element set V and an integer k ≥ 0, we show that the family of all sets X ⊆ V with f(X) = k admits a polynomial-size representation: it can be described by a list of at most O(n^{4k}) items, each consisting of a set to be included, another set to be excluded, and a partition of remaining elements, such that the union of some members of the partition and the set to be included are precisely all sets X with f(X) = k. We also give an algorithm that constructs this representation in time O(n^{2k+7}γ+n^{2k+8}+n^{4k+2}), where γ is the oracle time to evaluate f. This generalizes the low rank structure theorem of Bojańczyk, Pilipczuk, Przybyszewski, Sokołowski, and Stamoulis [Low rank MSO, LICS 2026] on cut-rank functions on graphs to general connectivity functions. As an application, for fixed k, we obtain a polynomial-time algorithm for finding a set A with f(A) = k and a prescribed cardinality constraint on A.

      Abstract
We study connectivity functions, that is, integer-valued symmetric submodular functions on a finite
ground set attaining 0 on the empty set. For a connectivity function f on an n-element set V and
an integer k ≥ 0, we show that the family of all sets X ⊆ V with f (X) = k admits a polynomial-size
representation: it can be described by a list of at most O(n4k ) items, each consisting of a set to be
included, another set to be excluded, and a partition of remaining elements, such that the union of
some members of the partition and the set to be included are precisely all sets X with f (X) = k. We
also give an algorithm that constructs this representation in time O(n2k+7 γ + n2k+8 + n4k+2 ), where
γ is the oracle time to evaluate f . This generalizes the low rank structure theorem of Bojańczyk,
Pilipczuk, Przybyszewski, Sokołowski, and Stamoulis [Low rank MSO, LICS 2026] on cut-rank
functions on graphs to general connectivity functions. As an application, for fixed k, we obtain a
polynomial-time algorithm for finding a set A with f (A) = k and a prescribed cardinality constraint
on A.

 1      Introduction
A connectivity function on a finite set V is a function f : 2V → Z satisfying the following
three conditions.
(a) (symmetric) f (X) = f (V − X) for all X ⊆ V .
(b) (submodular) f (X) + f (Y ) ≥ f (X ∪ Y ) + f (X ∩ Y ) for all X, Y ⊆ V .
(c) f (∅) = 0.
Here are several examples of connectivity functions. See [3, 8] for more instances of symmetric
submodular functions.
   Vertex cut: Given a graph G and a set X of edges, let ν(X) be the number of vertices
    incident with both an edge in X and an edge in E(G) − X.

          We prove the following theorem. This is motivated by the low rank structure theorem of
       Bojańczyk, Pilipczuk, Przybyszewski, Sokołowski, and Stamoulis [1, Theorem 6.1], which
       covers the special case of f being the cut-rank function of a graph.

       ▶ Theorem 1. Let f be a connectivity function on an n-element set V . Then for every
       non-negative integer k, there exists a collection {(Xi , Yi , Pi )}i∈I of tuples of disjoint subsets
       Xi , Yi of V and a partition Pi of V − (Xi ∪ Yi ) for each i ∈ I such that |I| ≤ O(n4k ) and
       {X ⊆ V : f (X) = k} is precisely equal to

       Furthermore, such a collection can be constructed in time O(n2k+7 γ + n2k+8 + n4k+2 ), where
       γ is the time to compute f (X) for any set X.

          As a corollary, for each fixed k, we obtain a polynomial-time algorithm to find a set A
       with f (A) = k and |A ∩ W | ∈ T if it exists, for an input connectivity function f on V given
       by an oracle and for a set W ⊆ V and a set T ⊆ {0, 1, . . . , |W |}. If T = {⌈|V | /2⌉} and
       W = V , then this is the submodular minimum bisection problem parameterized by the
       function value for connectivity functions.

       ▶ Corollary 2. Let f be a connectivity function on an n-element set V . Let W be a subset
       of V . In time O(n2k+7 γ + n2k+8 + n4k+2 ), for a set T ⊆ {0, 1, . . . , |W |} of integers, we can
       find a set A such that |A ∩ W | ∈ T and f (A) = k or confirm that there is no such set A,
       where f is given by an oracle that answers f (X) for any set X in time γ.

           This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls definitions of interpolations of a
       connectivity function and discuss several properties. Section 3 defines the blocking digraphs.
       Section 4 discusses our key lemma, saying that the blocking digraph cannot have a structure
       called a skew matching. Section 5 describes all closed sets in a directed acyclic graph, when
       there is no large skew matching. Section 6 finally presents the proof of the main theorem.
       Section 7 gives the proof of the corollary.

        2      Preliminaries
       Let us start this section by reviewing some terms on directed graphs, also called digraphs.
       A vertex of a digraph is called a sink if it has no outgoing arcs and it is called a source if
       it has no incoming arcs. For a set X of vertices, we write Out(X) to denote the set of all
       vertices y such that there is a directed path from a vertex in X to y. Similarly, we write
       In(X) to denote the set of all vertices y such that there is a directed path from y to a vertex
       in X. We write D[X] to denote the subgraph of D induced by X, that is the directed graph
       obtained by deleting all vertices outside of X and all arcs incident with a vertex out of X. A
       set X of vertices of a directed graph is independent if D[X] has no arcs.

     Now let us recall the definition of an interpolation of a connectivity function, introduced
in [7]. We write 3V to denote a set of disjoint subsets {(X, Y ) : X, Y ⊆ V, X ∩ Y = ∅}. Let
f : 2V → Z be a connectivity function. We say that f ∗ : 3V → Z is an interpolation of f if it
satisfies the following four conditions.
   (i) f ∗ (X, V − X) = f (X) for all X ⊆ V .
  (ii) (monotone) If C ∩ D = ∅, A ⊆ C, and B ⊆ D, then f ∗ (A, B) ≤ f ∗ (C, D).
 (iii) (submodular) f ∗ (A, B) + f ∗ (C, D) ≥ f ∗ (A ∩ C, B ∪ D) + f ∗ (A ∪ C, B ∩ D) for all
       (A, B), (C, D) ∈ 3V .
 (iv) f ∗ (∅, ∅) = f (∅).

▶ Theorem 3 (Orlin [5]). Let n be a positive integer. Let f : 2V → Z be a submodular
function on an n-element set V . Let us assume that γ is the time to compute f (X) for any

   Our aim is to describe subsets X of V with f (X) = k. The following two lemmas state
that if f (X) = k, then there will be a pair (A, B) of small sets such that A ⊆ X, B ⊆ V − X,
and f ∗ (A, B) = k.

▶ Lemma 4. Let r : 2V → Z be a submodular function such that r(X) ≤ r(Y ) for all
X ⊆ Y ⊆ V and r(∅) = 0. Then there exists a set X with r(X) = r(V ) and |X| ≤ r(V ).
Moreover, if we can compute r(Z) in time γ for any subset Z of V , then we can find such a
set X in time O(γ |V |).

Proof. We proceed by induction on |V |. This statement is trivially true if r(V ) = 0. Thus we
may assume that r(V ) > 0. Let v ∈ V . If r(V −{v}) = r(V ), then by the induction hypothesis
applied to V − {v}, there is a subset X ⊆ V − {v} such that r(X) = r(V − {v}) = r(V ) and
|X| ≤ r(V ), as desired. Therefore we may assume that r(V − {v}) < r(V ). By the induction
hypothesis applied to V − {v}, there is a subset X of V − {v} such that r(X) = r(V − {v})
and |X| ≤ r(V − {v}).
   For every w ∈ V − (X ∪ {v}), we have r(X) ≤ r(X ∪ {w}) ≤ r(V − {v}) = r(X), and
therefore r(X ∪ {w}) = r(X). Let Y be a maximal subset of V such that X ∪ {v} ⊆ Y
and r(Y ) = r(X ∪ {v}). If Y ̸= V , then for w ∈ V − Y , we have r(X ∪ {w}) + r(Y ) ≥
r(Y ∪ {w}) + r(X) and therefore r(Y ∪ {w}) = r(Y ), contradicting the assumption that
Y is maximal. Therefore, Y = V . This implies that r(X ∪ {v}) = r(V ). Note that
|X| + 1 ≤ r(V − {v}) + 1 ≤ r(V ). Thus X ∪ {v} is a desired set.                            ◀

▶ Lemma 5. Let f be a connectivity function on a finite set V . Let f ∗ be an interpolation
of f . Let X be a subset of V . If f (X) = k, then there exist A ⊆ X, B ⊆ V − X such that
max(|A| , |B|) ≤ k and f ∗ (A, B) = k. Moreover, if we can compute f ∗ (S, T ) in time γ for
any pair (S, T ) of disjoint subsets of V , then we can find such a pair (A, B) in time O(γ |V |).

Proof. We may assume that k > 0. For fixed V − X, the function A′ 7→ f ∗ (A′ , V − X) on
subsets of X is non-decreasing and submodular by the monotonicity and submodularity of f ∗ .

         7      Application to submodular minimum bisection
        The submodular minimum bisection problem is for an input connectivity function f on
        an n-element set V with an integer k to find a partition of V into two sets A and B such
        that |A| = ⌊n/2⌋, |B| = ⌈n/2⌉, and f (A) ≤ k.

    Recall that for a graph G and a subset X of V (G), η(X) is the number of edges between X
and V (G)−X. As discussed in Section 1, η is a connectivity function on V (G). The minimum
bisection problem for η was previously studied by Cygan, Lokshtanov, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk,
and Saurabh [2], who showed that it is fixed-parameter tractable.
    We would like to ask whether the minimum bisection problem for other connectivity
functions are fixed-parameter tractable. More generally is it true that the submodular
minimum bisection is fixed-parameter tractable for all connectivity functions?
